title: The clinical method: history, exam, diagnosis and evidence
note: Diagnosis is a reasoning process: the history and examination generate a ranked differential diagnosis, and tests are chosen to raise or lower the probability of each item. Sensitivity and specificity describe the test itself; predictive values also depend on how common the condition is in the people tested.

read.title: Why a positive test can still be wrong
text: Imagine a test with 90 percent sensitivity and 90 percent specificity, used to screen 1,000 people. If the condition is present in 1 percent of them, 10 people have it. The test catches 9 of them. Of the 990 people without it, 10 percent, or 99, also test positive. That gives 108 positive results, of which only 9 are true. The positive predictive value is about 8 percent.

Now use the same test in a clinic where half of the 1,000 patients have the condition. It catches 450 of the 500 who have it and falsely flags 50 of the 500 who do not. Of 500 positives, 450 are true, so the positive predictive value is 90 percent. Nothing about the test changed. Only the pretest probability did.

This is why clinicians think about who is being tested. A good history and examination raise or lower the probability of a condition before any test is ordered, and that starting probability shapes how much a result should change their thinking. It is also why a screening program for a rare condition expects many false positives and plans confirmatory testing for anyone who screens positive.
